topics.title: What is HTML & How the Web Works
topics.summary: HTML is the markup language that gives every web page its structure and meaning.
topics.description:
**HTML** stands for **HyperText Markup Language**. It is not a programming language – it is a *markup* language. You wrap content in tags to tell the browser *what that content is*: a heading, a paragraph, a link, an image, a form and so on. ### Hypertext and markup - **Hypertext** means text that links to other text. When you click a word and land on another page, that word is a *hyperlink*. This idea was invented by **Tim Berners-Lee**, who also built the first website. - **Markup** means annotating content with tags like `

` and `

` so software can understand its structure. ### The three layers of a web page | Layer | Language | Job | |---|---|---| | Structure | HTML | What is on the page | | Presentation | CSS | How it looks | | Behaviour | JavaScript | What it does | You cannot build a real website using only CSS and JavaScript – HTML is the foundation you must master first. ### How a page reaches your screen 1. You type a URL or click a link. 2. The browser sends an HTTP request to a server. 3. The server answers with an HTML file (usually `index.html`). 4. The browser **parses** the HTML into a tree called the **DOM**, downloads linked CSS/JS/images, and paints the page. ### File basics - Use the `.html` extension (`.htm` is the old 3-letter form from DOS days; both work). - A file named `index.html` is the default page of a folder, so the URL `example.com/` and `example.com/index.html` show the same page. - A site built only with HTML/CSS/JS is *static*. Adding a backend and a database makes it a *full-stack* (dynamic) site.
keyPoints: HTML = HyperText Markup Language; it describes structure and meaning, not logic.
HTML (structure) + CSS (style) + JavaScript (behaviour) make a web page.
The browser turns HTML into a DOM tree and renders it.
index.html is the default page served for a folder URL.
HTML is not case sensitive for tag names, but lowercase is the convention.
pitfalls: Calling HTML a programming language - it has no variables, loops or logic.
Using spaces or capital letters in file names - prefer lowercase-with-dashes like about-us.html.

topics.title: Document Structure: doctype, html, head, body
topics.summary: Every HTML page follows the same skeleton: doctype, html root, head for metadata, body for content.
topics.description:
Every HTML page, no matter how big, is built on the same skeleton. Learning it once means you can write any page from memory.

### The parts
- **`<!DOCTYPE html>`** - tells the browser "this is an HTML5 document". It has no closing tag and must be the very first line. Without it browsers switch to *quirks mode* and render in an old, inconsistent way.
- **`<html lang="en">`** - the root element. The `lang` attribute states the language of the content; it helps screen readers pick the right voice, helps translation tools and search engines.
- **`<head>`** - information *about* the page: title, character set, viewport, CSS links, SEO meta tags. Nothing in it is shown on the page itself (except the title in the tab).
- **`<body>`** - everything the visitor actually sees: text, images, forms, buttons.

### Important head items
- `<meta charset="UTF-8">` - the character encoding; put it first so special characters and emoji display correctly.
- `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">` - makes the page responsive on phones.
- `<title>` - text shown in the browser tab, bookmarks and search results.

### Rules to remember
- There is exactly **one** `<html>`, one `<head>` and one `<body>`.
- `<head>` comes before `<body>`, both inside `<html>`.
- Indent nested elements so the structure is easy to read.

Editors such as VS Code create this skeleton when you type `!` and press Tab (Emmet).
keyPoints: <!DOCTYPE html> must be the first line - it enables standards mode.
<html lang="..."> is the single root element.
<head> holds metadata; <body> holds visible content.
Always add meta charset and meta viewport.
Type ! then Tab in VS Code to generate the boilerplate.
pitfalls: Forgetting the doctype - the page renders in quirks mode.
Putting visible content inside <head> - the browser moves or ignores it.
Forgetting the lang attribute - hurts accessibility and SEO.

topics.title: Headings h1-h6
topics.summary: Six heading levels create the outline of a page for readers, search engines and screen readers.
topics.description:
HTML has six heading elements: `<h1>` (most important, largest) down to `<h6>` (least important, smallest). Headings are not just "big text" - they form the **outline** of your page.

### Why headings matter
- **Readers** scan a page by its headings.
- **Search engines** use them to understand what the page is about.
- **Screen reader users** jump from heading to heading to navigate, so the order must make sense.

### Rules to follow
1. Use **one `<h1>` per page** for the main title (the traditional, safest approach).
2. Go in order: `h1` → `h2` → `h3`. Do not skip levels (e.g. `h1` straight to `h3`) just to get a smaller size.
3. Choose a heading by *meaning*, then control the size with CSS.
4. Do not use headings just to make text bold or big.

### Default look
Browsers give headings a bold weight and a default size (`h1` ≈ 2em, `h2` ≈ 1.5em, `h3` ≈ 1.17em, `h4` = 1em, `h5` ≈ 0.83em, `h6` ≈ 0.67em) plus vertical margins. All of this can be changed with CSS.

### Example outline
```
h1 The Best HTML Course
  h2 Basics
    h3 Tags
    h3 Attributes
  h2 Forms
```
keyPoints: h1 is the most important, h6 the least; six levels in total.
Use a single h1 per page for the main topic.
Do not skip levels; keep a logical hierarchy.
Pick headings for meaning and use CSS for size.
Screen readers and search engines rely on headings.
pitfalls: Skipping from h1 to h4 because you like the font size.
Using <h1> for the logo and again for the page title.
Using <b> or a styled <div> instead of a heading for section titles.

topics.title: Quotes, Abbreviations, Time & More Inline Semantics
topics.summary: blockquote, q, cite, abbr, time, address, dfn, wbr and other meaningful text elements.
topics.description:
Beyond bold and italic, HTML has small elements that add precise meaning. They help accessibility, SEO and give you hooks for CSS.

### Quotations
- `<blockquote cite="url">` - a long quote set apart as a block.
- `<q>` - a short inline quote; the browser adds quotation marks.
- `<cite>` - the title of a work (book, song, film) being referenced.

### Terms and abbreviations
- `<abbr title="World Health Organization">WHO</abbr>` - shows the full form on hover and tells assistive tech.
- `<dfn>` - the defining instance of a term.

### Dates and times
`<time datetime="2026-10-14">14 Oct 2026</time>` gives machines an exact, machine-readable value while humans see friendly text. Search engines and calendars can use it.

### Contact info
`<address>` marks contact information for the nearest `<article>` or the whole page (author, email, postal address). It is *not* for any random address.

### Other useful inline elements
| Element | Use |
|---|---|
| `<wbr>` | A place where a very long word may break |
| `<bdo dir="rtl">` | Override text direction |
| `<data value="42">` | Machine-readable value for content |
| `<ruby>` | Pronunciation annotations (East Asian text) |

Every one of these is **phrasing content**: it sits inside paragraphs and does not start a new line.
keyPoints: blockquote = block quote, q = inline quote, cite = title of a work.
abbr + title gives the full form of an abbreviation.
time datetime="..." makes dates machine readable.
address is for contact details of the author/page owner.
wbr suggests where long words may wrap.
pitfalls: Using blockquote just to indent text - use CSS margin instead.
Wrapping the quotation marks yourself inside <q> (the browser adds them).
Using <address> for any postal address in the content.

topics.summary: ul for bullets, ol for numbered steps, li for each item and the attributes type, start and reversed.
topics.description:
Lists group related items. HTML has three kinds; this topic covers the two most used.

### Unordered list `<ul>`
Items have no order and show bullet points. Use it for menus, features, tags.

### Ordered list `<ol>`
Items where order matters - steps, rankings. Items are numbered automatically.

Each item is an `<li>` (list item). The only valid direct children of `<ul>` / `<ol>` are `<li>` elements.

### Ordered list attributes
| Attribute | Effect |
|---|---|
| `type="1 / A / a / I / i"` | Numbering style |
| `start="10"` | First number |
| `reversed` | Count downwards |
| `<li value="5">` | Force a specific number |

`start`, `type` and `reversed` work **only on `<ol>`**, not on `<ul>`.

### Styling markers with CSS
`list-style-type` accepts `disc`, `circle`, `square`, `none` (for ul) and `decimal`, `lower-alpha`, `upper-alpha`, `lower-roman`, `upper-roman` (for ol).

### Navigation menus
Menus are lists of links. Remove bullets and lay items in a row with CSS:

```css
.menu { list-style: none; display: flex; gap: 10px; }
```

A list-based nav is the standard markup pattern because screen readers announce "list of 4 items".
keyPoints: ul = bullets (no order), ol = numbers (order matters).
Only li elements are direct children of ul/ol.
type, start, reversed work on ol only.
Use CSS list-style-type to change markers.
Navigation menus are semantically lists of links.

topics.title: Link Attributes: target, rel, download & more
topics.summary: target, rel (noopener, nofollow), download, title, hreflang and how to style link states.
topics.description:
Anchors become powerful with a few extra attributes.

### target
Where to open the link:
- `_self` - same tab (default)
- `_blank` - new tab/window
- `_parent`, `_top` - used with frames
- a **name** - opens in the iframe with that name

### rel
Describes the relationship to the target.
- `rel="noopener"` - stops the new page from controlling yours via `window.opener`. Modern browsers add it automatically for `_blank`, but write `rel="noopener noreferrer"` for old ones.
- `rel="nofollow"` - asks search engines not to pass ranking (user-generated links, ads).
- `rel="sponsored"`, `rel="ugc"` - more specific hints for paid and user content.
- `rel="external"`, `rel="next"`, `rel="prev"`, `rel="alternate"`...

### download
`<a href="report.pdf" download="my-report.pdf">` asks the browser to save the file instead of opening it. It works for same-origin files and blob/data URLs.

### Other attributes
- `title` - tooltip, extra info (not a replacement for good link text).
- `hreflang` - language of the linked page.
- `type` - MIME type hint.
- `ping` - tracking URLs (rarely used).
- `aria-label` - accessible name when the link only contains an icon.
- `tabindex`, `accesskey` - keyboard behaviour.

### Link states in CSS
`a:link`, `a:visited`, `a:hover`, `a:focus`, `a:active` - never remove the focus outline without providing a replacement.

topics.title: Audio Element
topics.summary: Embed sound with audio, offer several formats with source and provide fallback text.
topics.description:
The `<audio>` element embeds sound in a page with built-in player controls - no plugin needed.

```html
<audio controls>
  <source src="podcast.mp3" type="audio/mpeg">
  <source src="podcast.ogg" type="audio/ogg">
  Your browser does not support the audio element.
</audio>
```

### Attributes
| Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `controls` | Show play/pause/volume UI |
| `autoplay` | Start automatically (blocked by most browsers unless muted) |
| `loop` | Repeat forever |
| `muted` | Start silent |
| `preload` | `none`, `metadata` or `auto` - how much to load in advance |
| `src` | Single file shortcut |

### Multiple sources
List several `<source>` children with a `type` (MIME type). The browser plays the **first** it supports. Any text inside `<audio>` is fallback for very old browsers.

### Formats
- **MP3** (`audio/mpeg`) - universal.
- **WAV** (`audio/wav`) - uncompressed, big.
- **OGG** (`audio/ogg`) - open, good compression.
- **AAC/M4A**, **WebM/Opus** - modern.

### Accessibility
Provide a **transcript** for spoken content. Avoid autoplay with sound - it surprises and annoys users, and browsers block it anyway.

### JavaScript API
`audio.play()`, `audio.pause()`, `audio.currentTime`, `audio.volume` and events such as `ended` allow custom players.

`<video>` embeds a media player for video files.

  <source src="movie.webm" type="video/webm">
  <track kind="subtitles" src="en.vtt" srclang="en" label="English" default>
  Your browser does not support the video tag.

- `controls` - show the player UI.
- `autoplay` + `muted` - autoplay only works for muted videos.
- `loop` - repeat.
- `poster` - image shown before playback starts.
- `width` / `height` - reserve the space.
- `preload` - `none` | `metadata` | `auto`.

| Format | MIME | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| MP4 (H.264) | `video/mp4` | Best compatibility |
| WebM (VP9/AV1) | `video/webm` | Open, efficient |
| Ogg | `video/ogg` | Rare today |

`<track>` adds a WebVTT text file: `kind` can be `subtitles`, `captions`, `descriptions`, `chapters` or `metadata`. Captions are essential for deaf users and also help people watching with sound off.

### Embedding vs hosting
Self-hosted files use `<video>`. For YouTube or Vimeo you embed their player through an `<iframe>` (see the iframe topic).

topics.summary: An iframe embeds another HTML page (YouTube, maps, widgets) inside your page.
topics.description:
An **inline frame** `<iframe>` is a nested browsing context: a complete second page shown in a rectangle of your page. Typical uses are YouTube/Vimeo players, Google Maps, payment widgets, ads and live code demos.

```html
<iframe src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/VIDEO_ID"
        width="560" height="315"
        title="Intro video"
        loading="lazy"
        allowfullscreen></iframe>
```

| Attribute | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `src` | URL of the page to embed |
| `srcdoc` | Inline HTML instead of a URL |
| `title` | **Required for accessibility** - describes the frame |
| `width` / `height` | Size |
| `loading="lazy"` | Load only when scrolled near |
| `allow` | Permissions: fullscreen, camera, autoplay... |
| `sandbox` | Restrict what the frame can do |
| `referrerpolicy` | What referrer to send |
| `name` | Target for links: `<a target="frameName">` |

- Many sites (Google, Facebook, banks) **forbid** embedding with the `X-Frame-Options` / CSP `frame-ancestors` header. Use the site's official embed URL instead.

- `frameborder` is obsolete; use CSS `border:0`.

Content inside the iframe tag is shown only by browsers without iframe support - practically never.

topics.description:
The `<table>` element presents **tabular data** - information with rows and columns, like a price list, timetable or score board. It must **not** be used for page layout (use CSS Grid/Flexbox for that).

### The building blocks
| Element | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `<table>` | The whole table |
| `<tr>` | A table **r**ow |
| `<th>` | A **h**eader cell (bold, centred by default) |
| `<td>` | A **d**ata cell |
| `<thead>` | Group of header rows |
| `<tbody>` | Group of body rows (main data) |
| `<tfoot>` | Group of footer rows (totals) |

### How rows and cells combine
A table is built **row by row**: each `<tr>` holds `<th>` or `<td>` cells. There is no "column" element for data - the columns come from the cells lined up in each row.

### Why thead/tbody/tfoot?
They give structure: browsers can repeat the header on each printed page, assistive technology understands the roles, and you can style groups easily (`tbody tr:nth-child(even)` for zebra stripes).

### Styling
Default tables have no borders. Add them with CSS. `border-collapse: collapse` merges double borders into one.

### Deprecated attributes
`border`, `cellpadding`, `cellspacing`, `bgcolor`, `align`, `width` on table elements are obsolete. Do all presentation with CSS.

topics.title: colspan & rowspan (Merging Cells)
topics.summary: Make a cell span several columns or rows to build timetables and grouped headings.
topics.description:
Sometimes one cell must be wider or taller than the grid - a title across all columns, or a "Lunch" break that spans the whole day. Two attributes handle this.

- `colspan="n"` - the cell stretches over **n columns** (to the right).
- `rowspan="n"` - the cell stretches over **n rows** (downwards).

### Counting rule
Every row must "add up" to the same number of columns. A cell with `colspan="3"` counts as three cells; a cell with `rowspan="2"` also occupies a slot in the next row, so that row needs **one fewer** cell.

### Example plan - a timetable
```
| timetable (colspan 7)              |
| hours (rowspan 4) | Mon Tue Wed ... |
|                   | math math ...   |
|                   | Lunch (colspan 6) |
```

### Tips
- Draw the grid on paper first and count cells.
- Do not leave a row with too many or too few cells - the table will look broken.
- Heavy use of spans makes tables hard for screen readers; add `scope` / `headers` (see the accessibility topic) or simplify the table.
- For header cells that group columns use `<th colspan="2" scope="colgroup">`.

### colspan vs CSS
colspan and rowspan describe **data structure**, so they belong in HTML; the visual look stays in CSS.

topics.title: Forms: form, label, input & Submitting
topics.summary: The form element collects user input; label and name make controls usable and submittable.
topics.description:
A **form** collects data from the user and sends it to a server (or handles it with JavaScript). It is the basis of logins, search boxes, checkouts and contact pages.

### Core pieces
- `<form action="/submit" method="post">` - the container. `action` is the URL that receives the data; `method` is `get` (data in the URL, for searches) or `post` (data in the request body, for sensitive or large data).
- `<label for="email">` - a caption **linked** to a control by id. Clicking the label focuses the input, and screen readers announce it. Labels are essential for accessibility.
- `<input id="email" name="email">` - a control. The **`name`** is the key under which the value is sent; an input without a name is **not submitted**.
- `<button type="submit">` or `<input type="submit">` - sends the form.

### Two ways to link a label
```html
<label for="user">Username</label>
<input id="user" name="user">

<label>Username <input name="user"></label>   <!-- wrapping -->
```

### Form flow
1. User fills controls.
2. On submit the browser validates (see validation topic).
3. The browser sends `name=value` pairs to `action` and loads the response - unless JavaScript calls `event.preventDefault()`.

### Button types
`type="submit"` (default inside forms), `type="reset"`, `type="button"` (does nothing by itself - use for JS actions).

Every control needs a name to be submitted.

topics.title: Text-like Input Types
topics.summary: text, password, email, number, tel, url and search give the right keyboard and validation.
topics.description:
The `<input>` element changes behaviour with its `type` attribute. Choosing the correct type gives you free validation and the correct mobile keyboard.

| type | Use | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | Single line text | default |
| `password` | Secret text | characters hidden |
| `email` | Email address | validates @ format, email keyboard |
| `number` | Numbers | `min`, `max`, `step`, spinner |
| `tel` | Phone numbers | numeric keypad, no format validation |
| `url` | Web address | must be a valid absolute URL |
| `search` | Search query | may show a clear (x) button |

### Useful attributes
- `placeholder` - hint text (never a substitute for a label).
- `value` - default value.
- `min` / `max` / `step` - numeric range.
- `minlength` / `maxlength` - text length.
- `autocomplete` - help the browser autofill: `email`, `username`, `current-password`, `new-password`.
- `inputmode` - choose the virtual keyboard (`numeric`, `decimal`, `email`...).

### Number vs tel
Use `type="number"` for quantities you add or compare. Use `type="tel"` (or text + pattern) for IDs, phone numbers and OTPs - you do not want a spinner and mathematical behaviour.

### Security
A password field only **hides the characters**. Always send passwords over HTTPS and never store them in plain text.

interview.q: Why is type="number" a poor choice for phone numbers?
interview.a: It adds spinners, strips leading zeros and rejects characters like + or spaces. Use tel or text with pattern.

interview.q: Does type="password" encrypt the data?
interview.a: No, it only masks the characters on screen. Use HTTPS to protect data in transit.

topics.title: Radio, Checkbox, Select & Datalist
topics.summary: Let users choose from options: one of many (radio, select), many (checkbox), or suggestions (datalist).
topics.description:
### Radio buttons
Choose **exactly one** option from a group. Radios are grouped by sharing the same **`name`**. Each needs its own `value`.

```html
<input type="radio" id="m" name="gender" value="male"> <label for="m">Male</label>
<input type="radio" id="f" name="gender" value="female"> <label for="f">Female</label>
```

### Checkboxes
Choose **any number** (zero, one or many). Checked ones are submitted. Use `checked` for a default. Checkboxes sharing a name submit multiple values.

### select + option
A drop-down list. `<option value="..">` holds the value; `<optgroup label="..">` groups options; `multiple` allows multi-select; `size` shows a list box.

### datalist
`<input list="countries">` plus `<datalist id="countries">` gives **suggestions** while typing - but the user may still type something else.

| | select | datalist |
|---|---|---|
| Free text allowed | No | Yes |
| Must pick from list | Yes | No |
| Best for | fixed choice | suggestions |

### Accessibility tips
- Wrap related radios/checkboxes in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>` (see next topic).
- Always connect each choice to a label so the text is clickable.
- For long lists of yes/no choices consider a checkbox group; for 2 mutually exclusive options a radio group.

topics.title: Date, Time, Color, Range, File & Hidden Inputs
topics.summary: Built-in pickers: date, time, month, week, datetime-local, color, range, file and hidden.
topics.description:
HTML5 added many input types that show native pickers, so you rarely need a JavaScript date library for simple forms.

| type | Control | Submitted value format |
|---|---|---|
| `date` | Calendar picker | `2026-10-14` |
| `time` | Time picker | `14:30` |
| `datetime-local` | Date + time | `2026-10-14T14:30` |
| `month` | Month & year | `2026-10` |
| `week` | Week of year | `2026-W42` |
| `color` | Colour chooser | `#e34c26` |
| `range` | Slider | a number |
| `file` | File upload | file(s) |
| `hidden` | Invisible value | any string |

### Constraints
`min`, `max`, `step` work on date/time/number/range. Example: `<input type="date" min="2026-01-01">`.

### file
- `accept=".pdf,image/*"` filters selectable types.
- `multiple` allows many files.
- `capture` hints the camera on mobile.
- The form needs `enctype="multipart/form-data"` and `method="post"` to upload.

### range
Has no visible value by default; show it with `<output>` and a few lines of JS.

### hidden
Sends data the user does not see (a CSRF token, a record id). It is **not secure** - users can edit it in DevTools.

### Browser support
All modern browsers support these pickers, but their UI differs. The submitted value format is always the same.

Submitted values use fixed ISO-style formats.

file uploads need method=post and multipart/form-data.
hidden inputs are not secret - never trust them.

interview.q: What is needed to upload files with a form?
interview.a: method="post", enctype="multipart/form-data" and an input type="file".

interview.a: No. It is only invisible; users can see and change it with DevTools, so always validate on the server.

topics.title: textarea, button & fieldset/legend
topics.summary: Multi-line text, proper buttons and grouping related controls with fieldset and legend.
topics.description:
### textarea
Multi-line text input. Unlike `<input>` it has a closing tag and its default text goes **between** the tags.

```html
<textarea name="msg" rows="5" cols="40" maxlength="300" placeholder="Your message"></textarea>
```

- `rows` / `cols` set initial size (or use CSS `width`/`height`).
- `wrap`, `maxlength`, `readonly`, `required` are supported.
- Whitespace inside the tags is preserved, so avoid indenting the content.

### button vs input
| | `<button>` | `<input type="submit">` |
|---|---|---|
| Content | any HTML (icons, text) | only the `value` text |
| Types | submit, reset, button | submit, reset, button |

Prefer `<button>`: it is more flexible. Always set `type` explicitly (`type="button"` for non-submitting buttons).

### fieldset and legend
`<fieldset>` groups related controls; `<legend>` is its caption. Assistive tech reads the legend before each control inside, which is critical for radio groups ("Gender, Male radio button").

```html
<fieldset>
  <legend>Contact Info</legend>
  ...controls...
</fieldset>
```

A `disabled` attribute on the fieldset disables **all** controls inside at once. Browsers draw a border by default; style it with CSS.

button can hold HTML; set its type explicitly.

topics.title: Built-in Form Validation
topics.summary: required, pattern, min/max, minlength and the Constraint Validation API validate without JavaScript.
topics.description:
HTML5 can validate forms **before** submitting - no JavaScript required. When a value is invalid the browser blocks submission and shows a message.

### Validation attributes
| Attribute | Checks |
|---|---|
| `required` | Value must not be empty |
| `pattern="regex"` | Value must match the regular expression |
| `min` / `max` | Numeric/date range |
| `minlength` / `maxlength` | Text length |
| `step` | Allowed increments |
| `type="email" / "url"` | Format |
| `multiple` | With email/file for lists |

```html
<input type="text" name="zip" pattern="[0-9]{6}" title="6 digit PIN code" required>
```
The `title` becomes part of the message when a pattern fails.

### CSS pseudo-classes
`:valid`, `:invalid`, `:required`, `:optional`, `:user-invalid` let you style states. Prefer `:user-invalid` (only after interaction) so fields are not red on page load.

### Constraint Validation API
- `input.validity` - a ValidityState (`valueMissing`, `typeMismatch`, `patternMismatch`...).
- `input.setCustomValidity("msg")` - set your own message (empty string clears it).
- `form.checkValidity()` / `reportValidity()`.

### novalidate
`<form novalidate>` switches the browser validation off so you can use your own JS validation.

### Never trust the client
Browser validation is a **convenience**. Always validate again on the server.
keyPoints: required, pattern, min, max, minlength, maxlength validate natively.
Use title to explain pattern requirements.
:invalid / :user-invalid style invalid fields.
setCustomValidity() customises messages.
Server-side validation is always necessary.

Forgetting to clear setCustomValidity("") - field stays invalid.
Styling :invalid on page load so everything looks like an error.

interview.a: Add novalidate to the form (or formnovalidate to a submit button).

interview.q: Why is client-side validation not enough?
interview.a: Users can bypass or edit it with DevTools or direct requests; the server must validate again.

topics.title: Form & Input Attributes: autocomplete, readonly, disabled...
topics.summary: autofocus, autocomplete, readonly vs disabled, form, multiple, enctype and other attributes explained.
topics.description:
Beyond type and name, many attributes fine-tune how controls behave.

### On inputs
| Attribute | Effect |
|---|---|
| `value` | Initial value |
| `placeholder` | Hint text shown when empty |
| `autofocus` | Focus on page load (use sparingly) |
| `autocomplete` | `on` / `off` / tokens like `email`, `one-time-code` |
| `readonly` | Cannot edit, **is submitted**, can be focused |
| `disabled` | Cannot edit or focus, **not submitted**, greyed |
| `required` | Must be filled |

| `form` | Associate with a form by id even outside it |
| `multiple` | Several files/emails |
| `accept` | File type filter |

### readonly vs disabled
This is a classic interview question: **readonly** values are submitted and focusable; **disabled** values are not submitted at all.

### On the form
- `action`, `method`, `enctype` (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data`, `text/plain`).
- `target` - where to show the response.
- `autocomplete`, `novalidate`, `accept-charset`, `name`.

### On submit buttons
`formaction`, `formmethod`, `formtarget`, `formnovalidate` override the form's settings for that button - handy for "Save draft" vs "Publish".

topics.title: output, progress & meter
topics.summary: Show calculation results, task progress and gauge values with built-in elements.
topics.description:
Three small elements display values and are often forgotten.

### output
`<output>` shows the **result of a calculation or user action**. Use `for="id1 id2"` to list the inputs it depends on and `name` so it can be part of the form.

```html
<form oninput="sum.value = Number(a.value) + Number(b.value)">
  <input type="number" id="a" value="3"> +
  <input type="number" id="b" value="4"> =
  <output name="sum" for="a b">7</output>
</form>
```

Screen readers announce changes (it has an implicit `role="status"`).

### progress
`<progress value="70" max="100">70%</progress>` shows **task completion**. Without a `value` it becomes an *indeterminate* spinner/bar (loading). The inner text is fallback.

### meter
`<meter>` shows a **scalar value within a known range** - disk usage, a score, battery. Not for progress!

| Attribute | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `min`, `max` | Range |
| `value` | Current |
| `low`, `high` | Thresholds |
| `optimum` | Ideal value |

The browser colours the bar (green / yellow / red) based on these thresholds.

### progress vs meter
- Progress: something is *being done* (upload 40%).
- Meter: a *measurement* (7 of 10 stars, 80% disk used).

The course's project page uses `<progress>` elements for skill levels - technically a `meter` would be more accurate there.

meter = a measurement in a range with low/high/optimum.
Always give an accessible label for progress and meter.

Forgetting to connect a label via for/id.

topics.title: Semantic HTML & Page Layout Elements
topics.summary: header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer describe the role of each part of a page.
topics.description:
A **semantic** element tells you what its content *is*, not just how it looks. `<div>` and `<span>` are non-semantic; `<header>`, `<nav>` and `<footer>` are semantic.

### Why semantics?
- **Accessibility** - screen readers can jump between landmarks (nav, main...).
- **SEO** - search engines understand which part is the main content.
- **Maintainability** - `<footer>` is easier to find than the 12th `<div class="x">`.
- **Free default behaviour** - e.g. keyboard and styling support.

### The main layout elements
| Element | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `<header>` | Introductory content / logo / heading of the page or section |
| `<nav>` | Major navigation links |
| `<main>` | The dominant content - **only one visible** per page |
| `<section>` | A thematic group of content, normally with a heading |
| `<article>` | Self-contained content that makes sense alone (blog post, news item, comment) |
| `<aside>` | Related but secondary content (sidebar, ads, tips) |
| `<footer>` | Footer of the page or section (copyright, links) |
| `<figure>`, `<address>`, `<time>` | More semantics |

### section vs article vs div
- Could it be syndicated on its own (RSS)? → `article`.
- A themed chapter with its own heading? → `section`.
- Only a styling wrapper? → `div`.

### Typical page skeleton
```
body
 ├ header (logo + nav)
 ├ main
 │   ├ article
 │   └ aside
 └ footer
```

Landmarks like `header` and `footer` map to ARIA roles *banner* and *contentinfo* only when they are direct children of `<body>`.

Use one main element per page.

The `<head>` holds metadata - data *about* the page. Order matters a little: put `charset` first.

### Elements allowed in head

topics.title: SEO Basics & Meta Tags
topics.summary: Help search engines understand and rank a page: title, description, headings, alt text and robots.
topics.description:
**SEO** (Search Engine Optimization) is making your pages easy for search engines to find, understand and show. HTML does a large part of it.

### The top on-page items
1. **`<title>`** - unique, descriptive, ~50-60 characters, keyword near the start.
2. **`<meta name="description">`** - a ~150-160 character summary shown under the title in results. It does not rank directly but boosts click-through.
3. **One `<h1>`** with a clear heading hierarchy below.
4. **Image `alt` text** and compressed images.
5. **Semantic HTML** and descriptive link text.
6. **Open Graph tags** for social sharing (next topic).

### Meta robots
`<meta name="robots" content="index, follow">` is the default. Use `noindex` to keep a page out of search results and `nofollow` to not follow its links. Per-link control: `rel="nofollow"`.

### meta keywords
`<meta name="keywords">` is **ignored by Google** today. It is harmless but pointless.

### More SEO factors
| Area | Tip |
|---|---|
| Content | Original, useful, matches search intent |
| URLs | Short, readable, hyphen separated |
| Mobile | Responsive layout + viewport meta |
| Speed | Optimised images, defer scripts, fewer requests |
| Links | Internal links to related pages, quality external links |
| Structure | `canonical`, sitemap.xml, robots.txt, structured data |

Good HTML cannot replace good content - it simply removes obstacles.

One h1 and a clear heading hierarchy.
alt text, semantic HTML and compressed images help.
robots meta controls indexing; keywords meta is ignored.
Mobile friendliness and speed are ranking factors.
pitfalls: Keyword stuffing in title/description.
Duplicate titles and descriptions across pages.
Accidentally leaving noindex on production pages.

topics.summary: Control how your page looks when shared on WhatsApp, Facebook, LinkedIn and X.
topics.description:
When someone pastes your URL into WhatsApp, Slack, LinkedIn or Facebook, the app fetches the page and reads **Open Graph** meta tags to build a preview card (title, description, image).

### Essential Open Graph tags
```html
<meta property="og:title" content="CodeRevise - Learn HTML Fast">
<meta property="og:description" content="Revise HTML from basics to advanced.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/cover.jpg">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/html">
<meta property="og:type" content="website">
<meta property="og:site_name" content="CodeRevise">
```

Notice they use **`property`**, not `name`.

### Twitter / X cards
```html
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<meta name="twitter:title" content="...">
<meta name="twitter:image" content="https://example.com/cover.jpg">
```
If Twitter tags are missing, X falls back to Open Graph.

### Image tips
- Use an **absolute URL** (https://...).
- Recommended size ~ 1200x630 px (1.91:1).
- Keep under ~5 MB; JPG/PNG are the safest.
- Add `og:image:alt` for accessibility.

### Testing
Social platforms cache previews. Use their debugger tools (Facebook Sharing Debugger, LinkedIn Post Inspector) to refresh.

### og:type values
`website`, `article`, `video.movie`, `profile`, `product`...

topics.title: Accessibility (a11y) Fundamentals
topics.summary: Build pages everyone can use: semantic HTML, labels, alt text, contrast and headings first.
topics.description:
**Accessibility** (written *a11y*: a + 11 letters + y) means people with disabilities - blind, low vision, deaf, motor-impaired, cognitive - can perceive, operate and understand your site. It also helps everyone: mobile users in sunlight, people with a broken arm, keyboard power users.

### The first rule of ARIA
"If you can use a native HTML element, use it." Native elements come with roles, keyboard handling and states for free.

### The practical checklist
| Area | What to do |
|---|---|
| Structure | Use landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) and a heading hierarchy |
| Images | Meaningful `alt`; `alt=""` for decoration |
| Forms | Every control has a `<label>`; group with fieldset/legend; helpful error text |
| Links & buttons | Descriptive text; links navigate, buttons act |
| Language | `lang` attribute |
| Media | Captions, transcripts; no autoplay with sound |
| Colour | Contrast ratio ≥ 4.5:1 for text; do not rely on colour alone |
| Keyboard | Everything usable with Tab/Enter/Space; visible focus |
| Motion | Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` |
| Zoom | Do not block pinch zoom; content reflows at 200% |

### WCAG
The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (A, AA, AAA) are the standard. Most laws require **AA**. Principles: **POUR** - Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.

### Test it
- Tab through the page with only a keyboard.
- Use a screen reader (NVDA, VoiceOver).
- Browser DevTools Accessibility pane, Lighthouse, axe.
keyPoints: Native semantic HTML solves most accessibility needs.
All functionality must work with a keyboard.
Provide text alternatives: alt, labels, captions.
Contrast 4.5:1 for normal text (WCAG AA).
WCAG principles: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust.
pitfalls: Using a div with onclick instead of a button.

topics.title: ARIA: roles, states & properties
topics.summary: WAI-ARIA adds accessibility information that native HTML cannot express, for custom widgets.
topics.description:
**ARIA** (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes that tell assistive technology what a custom UI element is and what state it is in. ARIA changes **only the accessibility tree**, not behaviour or appearance.

### The five rules in short
1. Prefer native HTML (`<button>` over `<div role="button">`).
2. Do not change native semantics unnecessarily.
3. All interactive ARIA controls must be keyboard operable.
4. Never use `role="presentation"` or `aria-hidden="true"` on focusable elements.
5. All interactive elements need an accessible name.

### Three attribute groups
| Group | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Roles** (what it is) | `role="tablist"`, `dialog`, `alert`, `navigation`, `button` |
| **Properties** (relationships/labels) | `aria-label`, `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-controls` |
| **States** (changing) | `aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `aria-checked`, `aria-hidden`, `aria-disabled`, `aria-live` |

### Frequently used
- `aria-label="Close"` - name for an icon-only button.
- `aria-labelledby="id"` - name from another element.
- `aria-describedby="id"` - extra description (e.g. an error hint).
- `aria-expanded="true|false"` - disclosure/menu state.
- `aria-live="polite"` - announce updates (status messages).
- `role="alert"` - important, immediate announcement.
- `aria-current="page"` - current link in navigation.

### Landmarks
Use `<nav aria-label="Main">` when there are several navs so users can tell them apart.

Wrong ARIA is worse than no ARIA - always test with a screen reader.

ARIA only changes semantics, not behaviour - you must add the keyboard support.
aria-label / labelledby provide accessible names.
aria-expanded and aria-live communicate changing state.
Never hide focusable elements with aria-hidden.
pitfalls: Adding role="button" to a div but no keyboard handling.
Redundant roles like <nav role="navigation">.

**Global attributes** can be put on **any** HTML element.

| Attribute | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `id` | Unique identifier (fragment links, JS, labels) |
| `class` | One or more CSS/JS hooks |
| `style` | Inline CSS |
| `title` | Advisory tooltip text |
| `lang` / `dir` | Language and text direction |

topics.title: Canvas: Drawing with JavaScript
topics.summary: The canvas element gives a pixel surface you draw on with the 2D context API.
topics.description:
`<canvas>` is a rectangular **bitmap** area that you paint with JavaScript. It is used for games, charts, image editing, particle effects and animations.

```html
<canvas id="c" width="300" height="150">Your browser does not support canvas.</canvas>
```

### Getting a context
```js
const canvas = document.getElementById('c');
const ctx = canvas.getContext('2d');
```
Other contexts: `webgl`/`webgl2` (3D), `bitmaprenderer`, `webgpu`.

### Basic drawing API
| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `fillStyle` / `strokeStyle` | Colour |
| `fillRect(x,y,w,h)` | Filled rectangle |
| `strokeRect`, `clearRect` | Outline / erase |
| `beginPath()`, `moveTo`, `lineTo`, `arc` | Paths |
| `fill()` / `stroke()` | Paint the path |
| `fillText(text,x,y)` | Text |
| `drawImage(img,x,y)` | Images |

Coordinates start at the **top-left** (0,0); x goes right, y goes **down**.

### Size
Set `width`/`height` **attributes** (the drawing buffer). CSS size only stretches the bitmap and makes it blurry.

### Animation
Use `requestAnimationFrame(loop)`: clear, update, redraw, repeat.

### Canvas vs SVG
Canvas is **pixels** (fast for thousands of objects, no DOM per shape, not accessible by default). SVG is **vectors** (scalable, each shape is a DOM node, stylable). For accessibility provide fallback text or ARIA on the canvas.

topics.title: Loading Scripts: defer, async & type="module"
topics.summary: Control when JavaScript downloads and runs so it never blocks HTML parsing.
topics.description:
By default a `<script src>` is **parser-blocking**: the browser stops building the page, downloads the file, runs it, then continues. That delays rendering. Two attributes fix this.

### The three modes
| Attribute | Download | Executes | Order | DOM ready? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (none) | blocks parser | immediately | in order | No |
| `defer` | parallel | after HTML parsed, before DOMContentLoaded | **in order** | Yes |
| `async` | parallel | as soon as downloaded | **unpredictable** | Maybe |
| `type="module"` | parallel | deferred by default | module graph | Yes |

### Choosing
- **App code that touches the DOM or depends on other scripts** → `defer` (put the tag in `<head>`).
- **Independent scripts** such as analytics or ads → `async`.
- **Modern ES modules** (`import`/`export`) → `type="module"`; it is deferred automatically, strict mode, own scope.
- Old habit: scripts at the end of body. `defer` in head is better because the download starts early.

### More
- `nomodule` - run only in browsers that do not support modules.
- `<script type="importmap">` - bare specifier mapping.
- `<noscript>` - fallback content.
- Inline scripts ignore `defer`/`async` (except modules, which are always deferred).
- Add `integrity` and `crossorigin` for CDN files (Subresource Integrity).

### CSS also blocks
Stylesheets in head block rendering (to avoid unstyled flashes) and block scripts below them. Keep CSS small and critical.

topics.title: Web Storage: localStorage & sessionStorage
topics.summary: Store key-value strings in the browser: persistent with localStorage, per-tab with sessionStorage.
topics.description:
Web Storage is a simple key-value store in the browser (about 5 MB per origin). It replaced many uses of cookies.

| | localStorage | sessionStorage | Cookies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lifetime | Until cleared | Until tab closes | Set by expiry |
| Scope | Origin (all tabs) | Origin + single tab | Origin (+ path) |
| Sent to server | No | No | Yes, with every request |
| Size | ~5 MB | ~5 MB | ~4 KB |

### API
```js
localStorage.setItem('theme', 'dark');
localStorage.getItem('theme');      // 'dark' (null if missing)
localStorage.removeItem('theme');
localStorage.clear();
localStorage.length; localStorage.key(0);
```

### Only strings
Convert objects with JSON:
```js
localStorage.setItem('user', JSON.stringify({ name: 'Asha' }));
const user = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('user'));
```

### The storage event
When another tab changes localStorage, a `storage` event fires in the other tabs - a simple way to sync tabs.

### Security & limits
- Synchronous (blocks the main thread) - keep data small.
- Readable by any script on the page, so **never store passwords or tokens** that XSS could steal (prefer HttpOnly cookies).
- Can throw in private mode or when full - wrap in try/catch.
- Use IndexedDB for large or structured data.

topics.title: Geolocation API
topics.summary: Ask the user for permission and read latitude/longitude with navigator.geolocation.
topics.description:
The **Geolocation API** lets a page learn the user's position (with explicit permission). It works only in **secure contexts** (HTTPS or localhost).

### Getting the position once
```js
navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(
  (pos) => {
    const { latitude, longitude, accuracy } = pos.coords;
  },
  (err) => console.log(err.code, err.message),
  { enableHighAccuracy: true, timeout: 8000, maximumAge: 0 }
);
```

### Watching movement
`navigator.geolocation.watchPosition(success, error, options)` returns an id; stop with `clearWatch(id)`.

### Error codes
| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 1 | PERMISSION_DENIED |
| 2 | POSITION_UNAVAILABLE |
| 3 | TIMEOUT |

### Options
- `enableHighAccuracy` - GPS (slower, more battery).
- `timeout` - ms to wait.
- `maximumAge` - accept a cached position this old.

### Good practice
- Ask only after a user action ("Find stores near me"), never on page load.
- Explain *why* you need it.
- Always handle denial and provide manual fallback (type your city).
- Location is sensitive personal data - do not store it without need.

### Permissions Policy
In an iframe the parent must allow it: `<iframe allow="geolocation">`.

topics.title: Drag and Drop API
topics.summary: Make elements draggable and handle dragstart, dragover and drop events.
topics.description:
The HTML Drag and Drop API makes native dragging of elements and files possible.

### Steps
1. Mark the source: `draggable="true"` (images, links and selected text are draggable by default).
2. Listen for **`dragstart`** on the source - store data with `event.dataTransfer.setData('text/plain', id)`.
3. On the target, handle **`dragover`** and call `event.preventDefault()` - this is what *allows* dropping.
4. Handle **`drop`** - call `preventDefault()`, read `getData()` and move/append the element.

### Events
| Event | Fires on | When |
|---|---|---|
| `dragstart` | source | drag begins |
| `drag` | source | repeatedly while dragging |
| `dragenter` / `dragleave` | target | pointer enters/leaves |
| `dragover` | target | continuously over the target |
| `drop` | target | released |
| `dragend` | source | finished |

### File drop
Dropping files from the desktop: read `event.dataTransfer.files` in the `drop` handler (and prevent the default so the browser does not open the file).

### dataTransfer
- `effectAllowed` / `dropEffect` - copy, move, link.
- `setDragImage()` - custom ghost image.

### Accessibility
Native drag and drop is mouse centred. Provide a **keyboard alternative** (buttons "move up/down", select + move).

For complex sortable lists many projects use libraries, but the native API is enough for simple cases.

topics.title: HTML Performance Best Practices
topics.summary: Make pages load and render fast: small HTML, optimised media, non-blocking scripts and good Core Web Vitals.
topics.description:
Fast pages rank better, convert better and work on slow phones. Much of the speed is decided by your HTML.

### What users feel - Core Web Vitals
| Metric | Meaning | Target |
|---|---|---|
| **LCP** Largest Contentful Paint | When the main content appears | ≤ 2.5 s |
| **INP** Interaction to Next Paint | Responsiveness to input | ≤ 200 ms |
| **CLS** Cumulative Layout Shift | Visual stability | ≤ 0.1 |

### Checklist
1. **Images**: right size, modern format (WebP/AVIF), `srcset`, `width`/`height`, `loading="lazy"` below the fold, `fetchpriority="high"` on the hero.
2. **Scripts**: `defer`/`async`, remove unused JS, avoid huge libraries for tiny jobs.
3. **CSS**: small critical CSS first, avoid `@import` chains, remove unused rules.
4. **Fonts**: `font-display: swap`, preload the key font, subset.
5. **Resource hints**: `preconnect` to key origins, `preload` only critical files.
6. **Third parties**: audit each one - ads and widgets are the usual culprits.
7. **DOM size**: avoid thousands of nested nodes; use semantic simple markup.
8. **Network**: HTTPS + HTTP/2/3, gzip/Brotli, caching headers, CDN.
9. **Media**: `preload="none"` for videos, poster images, no autoplay.
10. **Layout shift**: reserve space for images, ads and embeds.

### Measure it
Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights, WebPageTest and DevTools **Performance** + **Network** tabs. Test on a throttled mobile profile, not just your fast laptop.

### The simplest win
Every byte you do not send is free. Delete what you do not need.

topics.title: HTML Security: XSS, sandbox, noopener & CSP
topics.summary: Escape untrusted data, restrict iframes, protect links and know what Content Security Policy does.
topics.description:
HTML is where many web attacks land. Know the basics.

### 1. XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
Attacker-supplied text is inserted into the page and runs as script.
- **Never** put untrusted data in `innerHTML`, `document.write` or inline event handlers.
- Use `textContent` or escape: `<` → `<`, `&` → `&`, `"` → `"`.
- Sanitise rich text with a library (DOMPurify) or the Sanitizer API.
- Escape for the context: HTML body, attribute, URL and JS all differ.

### 2. Safe links
`target="_blank"` without `rel="noopener"` lets the new page access `window.opener` (reverse tabnabbing). Modern browsers default to noopener, but add it for clarity. Also validate user-supplied URLs - reject `javascript:`.

### 3. iframe sandbox
```html
<iframe src="https://thirdparty.example" sandbox="allow-scripts" title="Widget"></iframe>
```
An empty `sandbox` blocks scripts, forms, popups and same-origin access. Add back only what is needed: `allow-scripts`, `allow-forms`, `allow-same-origin` (never together with allow-scripts for untrusted code).

### 4. Content Security Policy
A header (or `<meta http-equiv="Content-Security-Policy">`) that whitelists sources of scripts, styles and frames:
```
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'
```

### 5. Other
- Subresource Integrity: `<script integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin>` for CDN files.
- `autocomplete` tokens, `type="password"`, HTTPS everywhere, no secrets in HTML or comments.
- `<form>` POST with CSRF tokens (server-side).

Use rel="noopener" with target="_blank".

Say the answer in one or two sentences, then give a tiny example. ### Basics | Question | Short answer | |---|---| | What is HTML? | HyperText Markup Language - the standard markup that structures web pages. | | Tag vs element? | Tag is the markup (`

`); element = opening tag + content + closing tag. | | What is the DOCTYPE? | Declaration that triggers standards mode (HTML5: ``). | | Void elements? | Elements without content/closing tag: br, hr, img, input, meta, link. | | Block vs inline? | Block starts a new line and takes the full width; inline flows in text. | | id vs class? | id unique, class reusable. | | div vs span? | Block generic container vs inline generic container. | | HTML vs HTML5? | HTML5 added semantic tags, audio/video, canvas, storage, forms, APIs and removed presentational tags. | | Is HTML case sensitive? | Not for tag and attribute names; lowercase is the convention. | ### Text, links, images | Question | Short answer | |---|---| | How many h1? | One main h1 per page is best practice. | | strong vs b? | strong = importance (semantic), b = visual boldness. | | Why alt? | Accessibility, fallback, SEO. | | _blank? | Opens in a new tab; add rel="noopener". | | mailto / tel? | Links that open email client / phone dialer. | | Absolute vs relative URL? | Full address vs resolved from the current location. | ### Forms and tables | Question | Short answer | |---|---| | GET vs POST? | URL query vs request body. | | readonly vs disabled? | readonly is submitted; disabled is not. | | Radio vs checkbox? | One of many vs many. | | select vs datalist? | Forced choice vs suggestions. | | thead/tbody/tfoot? | Group header, body, footer rows. | | colspan/rowspan? | Merge cells horizontally/vertically. | | th vs td? | Header cell vs data cell. |
keyPoints: Answer in one sentence, then give a mini example.
Know the pairs: tag/element, block/inline, id/class, div/span.
Know form pairs: GET/POST, readonly/disabled, select/datalist.
Mention accessibility and semantics where relevant.
pitfalls: Reciting definitions without examples.
Saying HTML is a programming language.
Forgetting to mention accessibility benefits.

interview.q: What is the difference between HTML and HTML5?
interview.a: HTML5 is the current standard that added semantic elements, native audio/video, canvas, SVG, new form controls, storage and many APIs, and dropped presentational tags.

interview.q: What are semantic elements? Give examples.
interview.a: Elements whose names describe their meaning: header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer, figure.

interview.q: How do you make a link open an email client?
interview.a: Use href="mailto:name@example.com".

interview.q: Why is the alt attribute required on images?
interview.a: It supplies a text alternative for screen readers, failed loads and search engines.

topics.title: Interview Questions: Advanced & Scenario-Based
topics.summary: Deeper questions about performance, accessibility, SEO, APIs and real-world scenarios.
topics.description:
These questions separate good candidates from great ones. Practise answering them with a reason and a trade-off.

### Performance and loading
| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| defer vs async? | Both download in parallel; defer runs after parsing in order, async runs ASAP in any order. |
| How to speed up a page? | Optimise images, lazy load, defer JS, preload critical assets, reduce DOM/CSS/JS, CDN and caching. |
| preload vs prefetch? | Current page high priority vs future navigation low priority. |
| What is critical rendering path? | HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM, combined into render tree, layout, paint. |
| What causes CLS? | Images/ads/fonts without reserved space. |

### Accessibility and SEO
| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| First rule of ARIA? | Use native HTML before ARIA. |
| How to make a custom button accessible? | Prefer button; else role, tabindex="0", key handlers, name, focus style. |
| How to make forms accessible? | Labels, fieldset/legend, error messages linked with aria-describedby, correct types. |
| SEO tags? | title, meta description, canonical, h1, alt, Open Graph, structured data, robots. |

### HTML5 APIs
| Question | Short answer |
|---|---|
| localStorage vs cookies? | 5 MB, client-only, persistent vs 4 KB, sent with each request. |
| Web workers? | Background threads without DOM access using postMessage. |
| What is Shadow DOM? | Encapsulated DOM/CSS subtree for web components. |
| canvas vs SVG? | Pixels vs vectors. |
| How does drag and drop work? | draggable + dragstart, dragover (preventDefault), drop. |

### Scenario questions
- **"A page looks tiny on mobile."** → missing viewport meta.
- **"Image causes layout jump."** → missing width/height.
- **"Link opens but the opener tab is hijacked."** → add rel="noopener".
- **"Form submits but the server gets nothing for a field."** → missing name attribute or disabled.
- **"Emoji shows as ???"** → missing UTF-8 charset.
- **"Two elements react to one label."** → duplicate ids.
keyPoints: Explain the critical rendering path in one breath.
Know async/defer, preload/prefetch, localStorage/cookies.
Have a debugging answer for common scenarios.
Always connect answers to accessibility and performance.
pitfalls: Memorising answers without understanding the reason.
Ignoring trade-offs (e.g. lazy loading everything).
Not mentioning testing/validation tools.

interview.q: Explain the critical rendering path.
interview.a: The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into a render tree, computes layout and paints. Blocking CSS/JS delays it.

interview.q: How would you make a div act as a button accessibly?
interview.a: Better to use a real button. Otherwise add role="button", tabindex="0", handle Enter/Space keys, give a name and visible focus.

interview.q: Why might a form field not reach the server?
interview.a: It has no name, is disabled, is outside the form without the form attribute, or is an unchecked checkbox/radio.

interview.q: How can you prevent layout shift from images?
interview.a: Set width and height attributes (or CSS aspect-ratio) so space is reserved before loading.
